source_text: Vitiari autem in unoquoque iam suo arbitratu vel bonum agente vel malum personae meritum dicimus, non naturae. Et ideo per gratiam Christi id sanari asserimus, quod vitiari potest, quoniam nec aliud sauciatum ostenditur, quam quod sanatum docetur.
pass_a_gloss: But to be vitiated in each one already by his own choosing, either doing good or evil, we say is the desert of the person, not of nature. And therefore we assert that through the grace of Christ that is healed which can be vitiated, since neither is another shown wounded than what is taught healed.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS meritum; Blaise; avoid later merit-theology
LS bonum; Blaise good-of-nature vs good-of-will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: We say that in each person already acting well or badly by personal choice, it is the person’s moral standing, not nature’s, that is corrupted. Accordingly we maintain that Christ’s grace heals what can be corrupted, since nothing is shown wounded except what is shown healed.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Context decides: Julian's forensic gratia is partiality; when he means divine help he still keeps 'grace' from the Latin, not later systems.
rejected: without grace as automatic (imports later soteriology)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
